title: David Dhawan Is Retiring After This Film. His Son Varun Is the Leading Man. Advance Bookings Are Already Open.
excerpt: Hai Jawani Toh Ishq Hona Hai opens Thursday with 50% off tickets and a father-son farewell that NRI audiences grew up with.
body:
There is a version of Bollywood comedy that exists primarily in the living rooms of Indian families abroad. It lives in the DVDs that travelled in suitcases from Mumbai to New Jersey, in the CDs that got passed around at Diwali gatherings in London, in the JioHotstar queues that NRI kids scroll through when they want to show their American roommates what their parents laughed at. David Dhawan built that version.

On Thursday, June 5, the 69-year-old director will release **Hai Jawani Toh Ishq Hona Hai**, his final film. He has announced his retirement. The leading man is his son, Varun Dhawan. The genre is the one David Dhawan made his own across four decades: loud, chaotic, unapologetically silly romantic comedy.

## The Last Dhawan Joint

The film follows Jass (Varun Dhawan) and Bani (Mrunal Thakur), whose five-year marriage has collapsed under the weight of career ambitions and disagreements about starting a family. After their separation, Jass travels abroad and falls for a new woman played by Pooja Hegde. What follows is the classic David Dhawan formula — misunderstandings piling on misunderstandings, confusion escalating into farce, and a resolution that wraps everything up with a hug and a song.

The supporting cast reads like a David Dhawan alumni reunion: Jimmy Shergill, Chunky Panday, Mouni Roy, Maniesh Paul, Rakesh Bedi, Ali Asgar, and Rajesh Kumar. Each presumably gets a signature comic set-piece. The CBFC has certified it U/A with a runtime of 2 hours and 16 minutes — lean by Dhawan standards, where chaos tends to expand to fill available screen time.

## A Career in Comedy

David Dhawan's filmography is a time capsule of Bollywood comedy from the 1990s onward. Hera Pheri, Judwaa, Bade Miyan Chote Miyan, No. 1 Ladkiwale — these films weren't critically celebrated in their time, but they became the shared cultural text of Indian families worldwide. For the diaspora specifically, these comedies served a function that serious cinema couldn't: they were the thing everyone in the room could watch together, from grandparents to grandchildren, without anyone reaching for the remote.

His collaboration with Govinda produced a run of films — Coolie No. 1, Hero No. 1, Partner — that defined an entire era. When that partnership ended, he pivoted to working with his son, producing Main Tera Hero, Judwaa 2, and Coolie No. 1 (the 2020 remake). The results were mixed commercially, but the father-son dynamic gave the collaborations an emotional weight that extended beyond the screen.

## Why NRIs Should Care

Hai Jawani Toh Ishq Hona Hai carries the weight of a farewell. David Dhawan isn't just retiring from directing; he's closing a chapter of Bollywood filmmaking that prioritised mass entertainment over critical approval. In an era where Hindi cinema is increasingly bifurcated — either ₹600-crore spectacles or intense Netflix-ready dramas — the mid-budget family comedy has nearly vanished. This might be the last time a filmmaker of Dhawan's generation delivers one in theatres.

The economics tell the story. Advance bookings opened on Monday with a promotional 50% discount on opening day tickets — a move that acknowledges the reality of theatrical comedy in 2026. The film has already been pushed from its original June 5 date to avoid clashing with Yash's Toxic, then back to June 5 after further shuffling. It will compete with Ram Charan's Peddi and Bobby Deol's Bandar for screens.

For diaspora audiences, the film will likely arrive in North American and UK theatres through Yash Raj Films or AA Films distribution. The comedy-entertainer genre has historically performed well in the NRI belt, where family outings to Bollywood films remain a weekend tradition.

## The Emotional Subtext

There is something quietly moving about a director choosing his final film to be a comedy starring his own son. David Dhawan has spoken in interviews about wanting to go out on a note that reflects who he is as a filmmaker — not chasing trends, not attempting a dramatic reinvention, but doing the thing he does best one last time.

Whether the film works or not is almost beside the point for long-time fans. The David Dhawan brand of comedy — broad, physical, relentlessly good-natured — belongs to a Bollywood that is disappearing. Hai Jawani Toh Ishq Hona Hai is both a movie and a monument to an era that the Indian diaspora carries in its bones.
author: Diaspora Desk
